Roman Shukhevych: Ukrainian nationalist militant (1907–1950). Shukhevych led some of the Galicia-Volhynia massacres, where tens of thousands of Polish civilians were killed.
This twelve-year Central American conflict, fought between a U.S.-backed government and the FMLN guerrilla coalition, formally ended with the 1992 Chapultepec Peace Accords — which conflict?
Salvadoran Civil War: 1979–1992 conflict in El Salvador.
A member of Japan's Liberal Democratic Party, this politician served as Deputy Chief Cabinet Secretary and State Minister for Foreign Affairs under the Third Abe Cabinet — who is he?
Discovered hiding in Guam's jungle in 1972, this Japanese army sergeant was one of the last WWII holdouts found nearly three decades after the fighting ended — who was he?
Shoichi Yokoi: Japanese World War II holdout (1915–1997)
This mythical creature combines a human head with a lion's body — in Greek myth she poses a fatal riddle to Oedipus, while in Egyptian tradition it's an unwinged, benevolent guardian — what is it?

Sphinx: Mythological creature with a human head and lion body. In Greek tradition, the sphinx is a treacherous and merciless being with the head of a woman, the haunches of a lion, and the wings of a bird.
Known by the art name Unam, this authoritarian leader served as South Korea's first president from 1948 until his resignation in 1960?
Syngman Rhee: President of South Korea from 1948 to 1960. Born in Hwanghae Province during the Joseon period, Rhee attended a local Methodist school, where he converted to Christianity.
The eldest son of a US president, this brigadier general received the Medal of Honor for directing troops at Utah Beach during the Normandy landings — who is he?
Theodore Roosevelt Jr.: American general and politician (1887–1944)
Hailed by the Senate as "the best ruler" and counted among the Five Good Emperors, this Hispania-born soldier pushed Rome to its greatest-ever territorial extent. Which emperor?
Trajan: Roman emperor from AD 98 to 117.
This philosophy and practice rejects treating animals as commodities, leading its followers to abstain from all animal-derived food, clothing, and entertainment. What is it?
This Warring States-era Chinese general commanded conquests of three rival kingdoms and is remembered by tradition as one of the four greatest generals of the late Warring States period — who was he?
Wang Jian (Qin): 3rd century BC Chinese military general.
Famous for pioneering sensationalist 'yellow journalism,' this publisher fought a fierce circulation war against Joseph Pulitzer's New York paper after acquiring a rival New York daily — who was he?
William Randolph Hearst: American newspaper publisher (1863–1951)
A former Palmach commando, this Israeli general became the first prime minister born in the region of Palestine — and was assassinated while serving a second term in 1995. Who was he?
Yitzhak Rabin: Prime Minister of Israel (1974–1977; 1992–1995)
A dispute between two rival lords escalated into a decade-long Japanese civil war from 1467 to 1477 that triggered the Warring States period — what was this conflict called?
Ōnin War: 15th-century civil war in Japan.
Which of these people was born first?
Benjamin Banneker (born 1731) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these four is the eldest?
Thomas Carlyle (born 1795) is the earliest of the four. Thomas Carlyle (4 December 1795 – 5 February 1881) was a Scottish essayist, historian and philosopher.
Which of these four is the oldest?
Fortran (founded 1957) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these four was founded earliest?

Fortran (founded 1957) is the earliest of the four. Fortran (formerly FORTRAN) is a third-generation, compiled, imperative programming language designed for numeric computation and scientific computing.
Who among these is a physicist?
Pick the chemist from these four.
Primo Levi is a chemist. Primo Michele Levi (Italian: [ˈpriːmo ˈlɛːvi]; 31 July 1919 – 11 April 1987) was a Jewish Italian chemist, partisan, Holocaust survivor and writer.
What is the atomic number of Copernicium?
Copernicium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Cn and atomic number 112.
What is the atomic number of Thallium?
Thallium is a chemical element; it has symbol Tl and atomic number 81.
In what year was Carlo Acutis born?
Carlo Acutis: Acutis was canonised on 7 September 2025, alongside Pier Giorgio Frassati.
In what year was Yulia Navalnaya born?
Yulia Navalnaya: The widow of Russian opposition leader Alexei Navalny, she has been described in media as the "first lady" of the Russian opposition.
In what year was Albert Einstein born?
Albert Einstein (14 March 1879 – 18 April 1955) was a German-born theoretical physicist best known for developing the known theory of relativity.
In what year did Pierre Curie die?
Pierre Curie (15 May 1859 – 19 April 1906) was a French physicist and chemist, and a pioneer in crystallography and magnetism.
In what year did Isaac Newton die?
Isaac Newton: Newton contributed to and refined the scientific method, and his work is considered the most influential in bringing forth modern science.
In what year was Sulfur discovered?
Sulfur (American spelling or sulphur (Commonwealth spelling) is a chemical element; it has symbol S and atomic number 16.
Diazepam: Pfizer. Diazepam, sold under the brand name Valium among others, is a medication of the benzodiazepine family that acts as an anxiolytic.
Boeing 777X: United States. The Boeing 777X is an American long-range, wide-body, twin-engine airliner built by Boeing Commercial Airplanes, undergoing flight testing.
Who is credited with discovering Microscopium?
Microscopium: Nicolas Louis de Lacaille. The name is a Latinised form of the Greek word for microscope.
Who is credited with discovering Toluene?
Toluene: Pierre Joseph Pelletier. Toluene is a colorless, water-insoluble liquid with a sweet smell, and is partially responsible for the aroma of gasoline and paint fumes.
Who is credited with discovering Pethidine?
Pethidine: Otto Eisleb. Pethidine, also known as meperidine and sold under the brand name Demerol among others, is a fully synthetic opioid pain medication of the phenylpiperidine class.
Who is credited with discovering Polonium?
Polonium: Marie Curie. Polonium is a chemical element; it has symbol Po and atomic number 84.
Born out of wedlock on the Caribbean island of Nevis and orphaned young, he became the first U.S. Secretary of the Treasury and founded America's first political party — who was he?
Alexander Hamilton (January 11, 1755 or 1757 - July 12, 1804) was an American military officer, statesman, and Founding Father who served as the first U.S.
This psychological term describes a diverse set of deficits in the ability to feel or anticipate pleasure, and is recognized as a diagnostic feature in the DSM-5 — what's the term?
Anhedonia is a diverse array of deficits in hedonic function, including reduced motivation or ability to experience pleasure.
This general medical term describes a joint disorder in which the smooth cartilage lining wears away, leaving bone to grind directly on bone during movement — what condition is it?
Arthritis is a general medical term used to describe a disorder in which the smooth cartilagenous layer that lines a joint is lost, resulting in bone grinding on bone during joint movement.
Marketed early on as the Debonair in its conventional-tail form, this piston single has been built continuously longer than any other aircraft ever made — which model?
Beechcraft Bonanza is an American general aviation aircraft introduced in 1947 by Beech Aircraft Corporation of Wichita, Kansas.

Native to eastern North America with resident populations as far north as Newfoundland, this crested songbird in the crow family has a black, U-shaped collar around its neck and a mostly white chest — name it?
Blue jay (Cyanocitta cristata) is a passerine bird in the family Corvidae, native to eastern North America.
This condition results from inflamed, fluid-filled sacs that cushion friction points between bones, tendons, and muscles, commonly striking the shoulder, elbow, hip, or knee — what is it?
Bursitis is the inflammation of one or more bursae in the body.
This American Nobel laureate coined the term 'bioorthogonal chemistry' and studies cell-surface sugars called glycans from her professorship at Stanford — who is she?
Carolyn Bertozzi (born October 10, 1966) is an American chemist and Nobel laureate, known for her wide-ranging work spanning both chemistry and biology.
Present naturally in breast milk and added to infant formula, this essential nutrient is also a building block for a neurotransmitter that controls muscle movement — which compound?
Choline is a cation with the chemical formula +.
This legless, non-venomous lizard native to Europe is often mistaken for a snake despite having smooth, non-overlapping scales and semi-fossorial burrowing habits — what is it called?
Common slow worm (Anguis fragilis) is a non-venomous species of legless lizard native to Europe.

Caused by prolonged exposure to glucocorticoids like cortisol, this collection of symptoms includes abdominal weight gain with thin limbs, a rounded red face, and weak, fragile skin that heals poorly — what's it called?
Cushing's syndrome is a collection of signs and symptoms due to prolonged exposure to glucocorticoids such as cortisol.

This is the practice of communication between representatives of states or institutions aimed at influencing international events, serving as the main instrument through which foreign policy goals are pursued. What is this practice called?
Diplomacy is the communication by representatives of state, intergovernmental, or non-governmental institutions intended to influence events in the international system.
This is the only surviving member of its order, the Proboscidea, and its tusks are actually overgrown incisor teeth used as both weapons and tools — what animal is it?
Elephant are the largest living land animals.
This Hungarian-American physicist won the 1963 Nobel for applying fundamental symmetry principles to the atomic nucleus, having once worked as an assistant to David Hilbert at Göttingen. Who was he?
Eugene Wigner (November 17, 1902 - January 1, 1995) was a Hungarian-American theoretical physicist who also contributed to mathematical physics.
Found at the terminal end of the limb in many vertebrates, this weight-bearing anatomical structure enables locomotion and is typically made up of multiple bony segments — what is it?
Foot (pl.: feet) is an anatomical structure found in many vertebrates. The plural form feet is an instance of i-mutation.
With the symbol Ge and atomic number 32, this lustrous, brittle metalloid was predicted to exist by Dmitri Mendeleev in 1869, decades before it was actually discovered — name this element?
Germanium is a chemical element; it has the symbol Ge and atomic number 32.
A French polymath dabbling in anthropology, medicine and physics, he's best remembered for an 1895 book that became a seminal work of crowd psychology — who was he?
Gustave Le Bon (7 May 1841 - 13 December 1931) was a leading French polymath whose areas of interest included anthropology, psychology, sociology, medicine, invention, and physics.
Serving as both Reichsbank president and Minister of Economics under Hitler, this economist was credited with Germany's 1930s 'economic miracle' even as he opposed aspects of rearmament — who is he?
Hjalmar Schacht (22 January 1877 - 3 June 1970) was a German economist, banker, politician, and co-founder of the German Democratic Party.
This medieval Arab scholar, considered a forerunner of modern sociology and economics, wrote his most famous work, an introduction to history known as the Muqaddimah, in just six months — who is he?
Ibn Khaldun (27 May 1332 - 17 March 1406, 732-808 AH) was an Arab scholar, historian, philosopher, and sociologist.

This American physicist worked on the Manhattan Project, then in 1949 proposed that — contrary to belief — not all atomic nuclei are spherical, an idea Aage Bohr later helped confirm. Who won a share of the 1975 Nobel for it?
James Rainwater (December 9, 1917 - May 31, 1986) was an American physicist who shared the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1975 for his part in determining the asymmetrical shapes of certain atomic nuclei.
One species of this succulent plant genus, native mainly to Madagascar, became one of the first plants ever sent into space aboard a Soviet space station in 1979 — what genus is it?
Kalanchoe (also called "kalanche" or "kalancho"), is a genus of about 125 species of tropical, succulent plants in the stonecrop family Crassulaceae, mainly native to Madagascar and tropical Africa.

Amphoteric and unreactive, this post-transition metal reacts with both acids and bases, melts at a low temperature, and tarnishes from shiny to dull gray in air — and three of its isotopes end major nuclear decay chains. Which element is it?
Lead is a chemical element with the symbol Pb (from the Latin plumbum) and atomic number 82.

Featuring a distinctive twin-boom design with a central pod housing the cockpit and guns, this American World War II fighter aircraft also served as a night fighter and long-range escort when fitted with drop tanks — which aircraft?
Lockheed P-38 Lightning is an American single-seat, twin-engined fighter aircraft that was used during World War II.
A sugar alcohol used both as a low-calorie sweetener and as a medication to reduce eye and brain pressure. It's poorly absorbed by the intestines. What's the name of this compound?
Mannitol is a type of sugar alcohol used as a sweetener and medication. It is unclear if use is safe in pregnancy.
Named in 1925 as an abbreviation of its chemical structure, this essential amino acid is required to kick-start protein synthesis — which amino acid is this?
Methionine (symbol Met or M) is an essential amino acid in humans.
These small, non-vascular, flowerless plants form dense green clumps or mats in damp, shady spots — name this group of plants?
Moss are small, non-vascular flowerless plants in the taxonomic division Bryophyta sensu stricto.
Found in tiny native amounts in Earth's crust but riding inside iron meteorites that never met oxygen, this hard, ductile metal shares its name with a small coin — which element is it?
Nickel is a chemical element; it has symbol Ni and atomic number 28.

Physicians in this medical specialty diagnose and surgically treat eye disorders — and can often spot signs of diseases elsewhere in the body just by examining a patient's eyes — what specialty is it?
Ophthalmology is the branch of medicine that deals with the diagnosis, treatment, and surgery of eye diseases and disorders.
This Scottish biologist-turned-town-planner coined the word 'conurbation' and his work contains one of the earliest versions of 'think globally, act locally.' Who was he?
Patrick Geddes (2 October 1854 - 17 April 1932) was a Scottish biologist, sociologist, Comtean positivist, geographer, philanthropist and pioneering town planner.
This anxiety disorder involves an irrational, excessive, and persistent fear of a specific object or situation, often leading sufferers to go to great lengths to avoid it — what is it called?
Phobia is an anxiety disorder, defined by an irrational, unrealistic, persistent and excessive fear of an object or situation.
Ranging from linear chains to heavily branched polymers, these carbohydrate compounds — like starch, glycogen, and chitin — consist of many simple sugar units linked together. What are they called?
Polysaccharide (from Ancient Greek (pols) 'many, much' and (skkhar) 'sugar') are "compounds consisting of a large number of monosaccharides linked glycosidically".

Harvested from the seeds of several Plantago species, this common dietary fiber supplement relieves both constipation and mild diarrhea, and occasionally doubles as a food thickener — what is it called?
Psyllium is the common name used for several members of the plant genus Plantago whose seeds are used commercially for the production of mucilage.

This genus of roughly 60 herbaceous perennials in the buckwheat family includes the familiar pie vegetable prized for its tart stalks despite mildly toxic leaves — which genus, native to Europe and Asia?
Rheum (plant) is a genus of about 60 herbaceous perennial plants in the family Polygonaceae.
Which plant genus in the mint family, comprising nearly 1,000 species of shrubs and perennials, includes both a common cooking herb and — surprisingly — rosemary as one of its species?
Salvia is the largest genus of plants in the sage family Lamiaceae, with just under 1,000 species of shrubs, herbaceous perennials, and annuals.
Setting a world record for mental calculation at London's Imperial College in 1980, this self-taught Indian prodigy also wrote books on math, puzzles, and astrology — who is she?
Shakuntala Devi (4 November 1929 - 21 April 2013) was an Indian mental calculator, astrologer, and writer, popularly known as the "Human Computer".
Beginning with stem cells near the basement membrane and passing through two rounds of meiosis, this process turns germ cells into haploid sperm inside the seminiferous tubules — what is it called?
Spermatogenesis is the process by which haploid spermatozoa develop from germ cells in the seminiferous tubules of the testicle.
This Chinese physician and revolutionary led the 1911 Revolution, overthrew the Qing dynasty, and founded the Republic of China as its first president. Who was he?
Sun Yat-sen (12 November 1866 - 12 March 1925) was a Chinese physician, revolutionary and political philosopher who founded the Republic of China (ROC) and the Kuomintang (KMT).
A metabolite of caffeine processed in the liver, this bitter alkaloid is the main one in the cacao plant and turns up in chocolate, tea, and kola nuts. What is it?
Theobromine is the principal alkaloid of Theobroma cacao (cacao plant).
Latin for 'three-headed,' this large muscle on the back of the upper arm has three parts, one of which also crosses the shoulder joint — name the muscle?
Triceps (Latin for "three-headed muscle of the arm"), is a large muscle on the back of the upper limb of many vertebrates.
First glimpsed in 1892 through tobacco-plant disease and counted as the most numerous biological entity on Earth, this submicroscopic agent can only replicate inside a living cell. What is it?
Virus is a submicroscopic infectious agent that replicates only inside the living cells of an organism.

This unit of time is based on how long Earth takes to complete one full orbit around the Sun, with the precise scientific definition running about 365 days, 5 hours, and 48 minutes — what unit is this?

Year is a unit of time based on how long it takes the Earth to orbit the Sun. In scientific use, the tropical year (approximately 365 solar days, 5 hours, 48 minutes, 45 seconds) and the sidereal year (about 20 minutes longer) are more exact.
Also called sweet flag, this wetland plant contains psychoactive compounds and has been banned from American food products despite centuries of use in traditional medicine — which species?
Acorus calamus: Species of plant. Acorus calamus (also called sweet flag, sway or muskrat root, among many other common names) is a species of flowering plant with psychoactive chemicals.
This congenital condition causes a total or partial absence of pigment, leading to white hair, pale skin, and often pink or reddish eyes — what is it called?
Albinism: Disorder causing lack of pigmentation.
Native to North America but now invasive across Europe after being introduced, this semiaquatic mustelid preys on rodents, fish, and frogs — which animal?
American mink: Semiaquatic species of mustelid. Because of range expansion, the American mink is classed as a least-concern species by the IUCN.
Evolved from vespoid wasp ancestors in the Cretaceous, these insects are easily spotted by their elbowed antennae and slender, node-waisted bodies — what are they?
Ant: Family of insects. Nearly all ant colonies also have some fertile males called "drones" and one or more fertile females called "queens" (gynes).
Caused by excessive exposure to silver dust or compounds, this condition turns the skin a striking blue or blue-gray shade, especially in sun-exposed areas — what's it called?
Argyria: Medical condition. The most dramatic symptom of argyria is that the skin turns blue or blue-gray, and is usually most prominent in sun-exposed areas of the skin.
Native to tropical Southeast Asia, this small tree bears bell-shaped rose-to-purple flowers and a ridged fruit that forms star-shaped slices when cut crosswise — which species?
Averrhoa carambola: Species of tree. It is a small tree or shrub that grows 5 to 12 m (16 to 39 ft) tall, with rose to red-purple flowers.

Nicknamed 'Huey,' this American utility helicopter became the first turbine-powered rotorcraft in U.S. military service, developed in the 1950s to meet an Army need for medical evacuation and utility missions. Which aircraft?
Bell UH-1 Iroquois: Huey family of American military utility helicopters.
This organ stores urine received from the kidneys via the ureters before it exits through the urethra, and gives us the medical term 'cystitis' when inflamed — what is it?
Bladder: Organ in vertebrates that collects and stores urine from the kidneys before disposal.
Named from Greek words for 'slow' and 'heart,' this condition means a resting heart rate under 60 beats per minute — sometimes normal in well-conditioned athletes — which condition?
Bradycardia: Heart rate below the normal range.
Common in cancer, heart failure, and other serious illnesses, this syndrome causes muscle wasting that better nutrition alone can't reverse — what is it?
In 1886 this German engineer patented what's considered the first practical automobile, and his Mannheim company later merged with Daimler — who is he?
Carl Benz: German designer and engineer (1844–1929)
Documented anatomically since the time of Hippocrates over 2,000 years ago, this roughly 4-centimeter-long fibromuscular organ connects the vagina to the uterine cavity. What structure is this?
Cervix: Lower part of the uterus in the female reproductive system.
This complex of DNA and histone proteins packages long strands of genetic material into compact structures while controlling access for transcription, replication and repair — what is it?
Chromatin: Complex of DNA and protein in eukaryotic cells.
This genus of demersal fish, named by Linnaeus in 1758, includes an Atlantic and a Pacific species prized for their mild flavor and flaky white flesh — what fish is it?
Cod: Common name for several fish, but mainly the demersal genus Gadus.
With a long hooked bill and webbing between all four toes, this fish-eating aquatic bird family includes the 'great' species commonly seen around Britain and Ireland — what are they called?
Cormorant: Family of aquatic birds. The common names "cormorant" and "shag" have been assigned to different species in the family somewhat haphazardly.
Sometimes called 'bipolar III,' this mood disorder involves cycling periods of mild depression and elevated mood that never reach the severity of full manic or depressive episodes — what is it?
Cyclothymia: Mental disorder. Cyclothymia differs from bipolar disorder in the fact that major depression and mania are not found.
Whether for an object, a process, or a system, this is the intentional concept or proposal created by a thinking agent, balancing purpose, aesthetics, and constraints — what single word names it?
Design: Plan for the construction of an object or system.
Brought to Australia as an infant, this geologist joined Shackleton's Nimrod Expedition and became a leading figure of the Heroic Age of Antarctic exploration — who is it?
Douglas Mawson: Australian geologist and explorer of the Antarctic (1882–1958)

Carried out mainly at power plants, this process transforms heat from burning fuel or nuclear fission — or the motion of water and wind — into power used by homes and businesses. What is this process called?
Electricity generation: Process of generating electrical power.
He coined the term 'quantum entanglement' in 1935 and shared the 1933 Nobel Prize in Physics with Paul Dirac for his work on atomic theory — who is he?

Native to a huge swath of Eurasia but declared a noxious species in New South Wales after damaging native fish, this predatory freshwater game fish is known locally in Australia as 'redfin' — which fish?
The discipline that studies money, currency, assets, and liabilities, divided into personal, corporate, and public branches — what is this field of study called?
Finance: Academic discipline studying businesses and investments.

Coated in cornmeal and pan-cooked while still unripe, this dish was originally a Northeastern and Midwestern staple before a hit movie rebranded it as quintessentially Southern comfort food — what is it?
Fried green tomatoes: American dish. Fried green tomatoes is a culinary dish usually found in the United States, made from unripe (green) tomatoes coated with cornmeal and fried.

Arriving late to a lecture, this mathematician copied down two famous unsolved problems in statistics, mistook them for homework — and solved them; he's better known for inventing the simplex algorithm for linear programming. Who was he?
Credited alongside Isaac Newton with inventing calculus, this German polymath also pioneered binary arithmetic and earned the nickname 'the last universal genius' — who is he?
This protein filament that grows from follicles in the skin is one of the defining traits of mammals, and its removal or styling carries different meanings across cultures — what is it?
Hair: Protein filament that grows from follicles found in the dermis, or skin.
Nicknamed for its shaggy white spines that dangle over a centimeter long, this edible mushroom is commonly called lion's mane and is used in traditional Chinese medicine — which fungus?
Hericium erinaceus: Edible mushroom. Hericium erinaceus, commonly known as lion's mane, yamabushitake, bearded tooth fungus, or bearded hedgehog, is a species of tooth fungus.
This climbing, hemp-family plant's female cone-shaped flowers are used to flavor and preserve beer — what's the scientific name for hops?
Humulus lupulus: Species of flowering plant.
Named from an Ancient Greek word for 'intestinal obstruction,' this medical condition disrupts the gut's normal propulsive movement, whether from lost peristalsis or a physical blockage — what is it?
Ileus: Disruption to the propulsive ability of the intestine.
A self-taught rocketeer and practicing occultist, this co-founder of both JPL and Aerojet invented the first castable composite rocket propellant before dying young in 1952. Who was he?
Court astronomer and advisor to Elizabeth I, this mathematician-occultist kept one of England's largest libraries and is credited with coining the term "British Empire" — who was he?
John Dee: English scientist and occultist (1527–1608/09)
Convicted in 1995 of fraud and illegally intercepting communications, this hacker served five years in prison before founding his own computer-security consulting firm — who is he?
Described both as a science and as the art of justice, this set of enforced rules can be made by legislatures, executive decrees or judges' precedent — what is it?
A sweet, aromatic flavouring used in confectionery, tobacco, and pharmaceuticals comes from the root of which legume — though more than a couple of milligrams per kilo a day can cause trouble?
Often a complication of cancer treatment, this incurable, progressive swelling condition is managed with compression therapy and manual drainage rather than diuretics — what is it?
Lymphedema: Swelling due to a compromised lymphatic system.

The first woman to write a mathematics handbook and the first appointed as a university math professor, this Milanese scholar later traded calculus for four decades of theology and charity — who is she?
Maria Gaetana Agnesi: Italian mathematician and philanthropist (1718–1799)
Typically running 21 to 35 days, this coordinated dance of estrogen and progesterone prepares the uterine lining and releases an egg to make pregnancy possible — what is it?
Menstrual cycle: Natural changes in the human female reproductive system.

Soviet pilots called it the "Balalaika" because its planform looked like the stringed instrument, while Poles dubbed it "Ołówek" — the pencil — for its slender fuselage; which most-produced supersonic jet in history earned all those nicknames?
Mikoyan-Gurevich MiG-21: 1956 Soviet fighter aircraft family.
Native to northern India, this fast-growing, drought-resistant tree is nicknamed the 'drumstick tree' for its seed pods and the 'horseradish tree' for its pungent roots — what is it?
Moringa oleifera: Species of flowering tree.
Sold as Aleve, this NSAID eases pain, fever, and menstrual cramps for up to twelve hours, and also comes in a more soluble sodium form — which drug?
Naproxen: Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) used to treat pain.
Known informally as bedwetting, this involuntary condition rarely stems from a specific medical cause and is often treated with alarms or hormone therapy — what is it called medically?
Nocturnal enuresis: Involuntary urination while asleep.
This biological process turns a primary oocyte into an egg cell capable of developing once fertilized, beginning during embryonic development — what is it called?
Oogenesis: Egg cell production process. Oogenesis or ovogenesis is the differentiation of the ovum (egg cell) into a cell competent to further develop when fertilized.
Sold under the brand name Protonix, this proton-pump inhibitor treats ulcers and acid reflux but can, with long-term use, cause vitamin B12 deficiency and low magnesium — what is this drug?
This genus of fungi is responsible for both a groundbreaking antibiotic and the mold that ripens certain blue cheeses — which genus?
Whether captured chemically on light-sensitive film or electronically by an image sensor, this art is fundamentally the practice of recording light — what is it?
Photography: Art and practice of creating images by recording light.
With a half-life of just 138 days, this rare radioactive element occurs only in trace amounts within uranium ore and is chemically similar to selenium — what is it?
Polonium: Chemical element with atomic number 84 (Po)
Encompassing peaches, cherries, plums, and almonds, this genus of flowering trees and shrubs in the rose family produces stone fruits called drupes — which genus?
Prunus: Genus of trees and shrubs.
Botanically a kin of spinach rather than a true grass, this protein-rich Andean pseudocereal was first cultivated near Lake Titicaca thousands of years ago — what is it?
Quinoa: Edible plant in the family Amaranthaceae.
Aristotle called this ancient art 'the faculty of observing the available means of persuasion,' identifying logos, pathos, and ethos as its three key appeals — which discipline?
Rhetoric: Art of persuasion. It is one of the three ancient arts of discourse (trivium) of classical antiquity, along with grammar and logic/dialectic.

Named after the naturalist who first studied it and described in 1797, this extremely venomous South Asian snake is notorious for its excruciatingly painful bite and ranks among the region's 'Big Four' — what snake is it?
Russell's viper: Species of venomous snake. Russell's viper (Daboia russelii) is a species of highly venomous snake in the family Viperidae.
Driven by an empirical cycle of observation, hypothesis, testing, and conclusion, this systematic discipline splits into natural and social branches. What is it?
Science: Systematic endeavour to gain knowledge.
Called the 'father of modern differential geometry,' this Chinese-born American mathematician and poet was honored with a medal the IMU named after him in 2010 — who is he?

Shiing-Shen Chern: Chinese-American mathematician and poet. Shiing-Shen Chern (Chinese: 陳省身; pinyin: Chén Xǐngshēn; October 26, 1911 – December 3, 2004) was a Chinese-born American mathematician and poet.
First isolated in 1820 from black nightshade berries, this glycoalkaloid poison also occurs naturally in potatoes as a built-in pest defense. What compound is it?
Solanine: Glycoalkaloid poison found in the nightshade family of plants.
Hired by Bill Gates in 1980 after leaving Stanford's MBA program, this businessman succeeded Gates as CEO in 2000 and now owns the Los Angeles Clippers — who is he?
Steve Ballmer: American businessman and investor (born 1956)
Closely related to privet and native from southeastern Europe to eastern Asia, which flowering shrub genus, commonly called lilacs, hosts caterpillars like the privet hawk moth?
Syringa: Genus of flowering plants in the lilac family.
Named from Greek for 'four teeth,' this family includes the pufferfish, blowfish, and toadfish — many of them among the most poisonous vertebrates alive. What is this family called?
Tetraodontidae: Family of pufferfish. Tetraodontidae is a family of marine and freshwater fish in the order Tetraodontiformes.

Sold under the brand name Zanaflex, this alpha-2 adrenergic agonist treats muscle spasticity from spinal cord injuries and multiple sclerosis, and racked up over 8 million US prescriptions in 2023 — what is it?
Nicknamed 'Crusty' by NATO, this twin-engined Soviet airliner featured a glazed nose and could operate from unpaved airfields — which aircraft is it?
The brightest star in the constellation Lyra, this star sits just 25 light-years away and served as Earth's northern pole star around 12,000 BCE — which star?
Vega: Brightest star in the constellation Lyra. It has the Bayer designation α Lyrae, which is Latinised to Alpha Lyrae and abbreviated Alpha Lyr or α Lyr.
Nicknamed the 'cock-of-the-woods,' this ground-dwelling grouse is the largest of all its kind, with males growing to nearly twice the size of females — which bird?
